explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think so, friend, since Israel is about to cross over there. But the text says Moses set these cities aside "…across the Jordan to the east" (Deuteronomy 4:41). That's the side Israel is standing on right now. Moses already said he won't be crossing the Jordan himself (Deuteronomy 4:22), so these cities are the ones he gets to set apart before the crossing.

That's right, friend. Moses sets these cities aside "…across the Jordan to the east" (Deuteronomy 4:41). They're not in the land Israel is about to cross into. I think that's worth a pause, because Moses says he won't be crossing the Jordan himself (Deuteronomy 4:22), and here he is doing a job on the side he'll stay on.

explanations.answer: One who did it by accident with no grudge
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says a manslayer could flee there after killing his neighbor "…unintentionally without prior malice." (Deuteronomy 4:42). No grudge, no plan, no malice beforehand. I think this is a heavy one, but the text is clear about who the cities were for.

explanations.answer: One who planned it for weeks ahead
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. The text says the city was for a man who killed his neighbor "…unintentionally without prior malice." (Deuteronomy 4:42). Planning something for weeks is the opposite of unintentional. That's not the man the verse describes.

explanations.answer: One who did it to take the man's land
explanations.explanation: Not this one, baker. Taking someone's land is a reason, and a reason means he meant to do it. The verse says the man killed his neighbor "…unintentionally without prior malice." (Deuteronomy 4:42). That's the only kind of man the text says could flee to these cities.

Yes, baker, life. The text says "To save one’s own life, he could flee to one of these cities…" (Deuteronomy 4:42). It doesn't say why his life was in danger, so I won't guess. What it does say is plain: running to one of these cities was how he could save it.

Good guess, friend, and I'll admit "home" sounds right. But the verse says he flees "To save one’s own life…" (Deuteronomy 4:42). The word is life, not home. The text doesn't say where he was when he started running, and it doesn't say what happens to the house. Home I could bake a new one out of dough, but life is the thing on the line here.

I get the thinking, baker. A good name matters a lot. But the verse says the man could flee "To save one’s own life…" (Deuteronomy 4:42). Life is the word in the text, and it's a bigger deal than any name, even one carved on a stamper handle.

That's right, baker, and look at that lineup. Bezer belongs to the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead to the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan to the Manassites (Deuteronomy 4:43). Three cities, three tribes, and nobody had to share a cookie box. Moses sets the cities aside, and the verse puts a tribe's name on each one.

A king of Moab? Friend, I looked all over that verse and he never shows up! Moses sets aside three cities, and each one belongs to a tribe: Bezer to the Reubenites, Ramoth to the Gadites, Golan to the Manassites (Deuteronomy 4:43). No king, no crown, no royal oven. I almost wish he was in there, though, because that would've been a wild twist.

Close to home, but no, baker. Moses sets these cities aside, but he doesn't own them. The verse says Bezer belongs to the Reubenites, Ramoth to the Gadites, and Golan to the Manassites (Deuteronomy 4:43). Moses is the one naming them, not the one holding the deed.
